 Total State Highway Fund Revenue Drops
 Oregon’s state and local transportation agencies are funded by the State Highway Fund, which includes revenues from the gas tax, driver and vehicle fees collected at DMV and from taxes paid by heavy trucks, and soon the per-mile road usage charge. The State Highway Fund is now declining with total revenue from January to September of this year coming in below 2025 levels by $32 million or 2.4%.
 Oregon Department of Transportation economists had long predicted gas tax revenue would decline as Oregonians purchase more efficient vehicles and use less gas to travel. That decline began earlier this year with motor fuels tax revenue down 2.2% for 2026 compared to the first nine months of 2025​. ODOT communicated about the decline in gas tax revenue and its causes earlier this month .
 In addition to gas tax declines, driver and vehicle fee revenues are also down $14.7 million for the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period last year. Registration and title fee revenues are down $7.7 million, while driver license fees are down about $6 million. Vehicle sales have been slow, reducing revenue from title and registration transactions. Driver license fees are lower than in 2025 as fewer Oregonians are choosing to renew their licenses early to get a Real ID.
 Starting in 2027, as directed by the Oregon Legislature in HB 3991, electric and hybrid vehicle owners will now be required to pay either two cents per mile or $340 per year. This road usage charge (RUC) program will be implemented in phases and is expected to be bringing in revenue from more than 500,000 drivers by mid-2030. However, even with the new revenue from RUC, ODOT’s latest revenue forecast projects total revenue in the State Highway Fund will still be below 2025 levels through 2029. Through 2035, revenue is expected to grow an average of less than eight tenths of one percent per year—well under the rate of inflation.
 ODOT and local governments will have about the same amount of revenue from the State Highway Fund in 2035 as they do today. After factoring in inflation, this revenue will buy about 20% less than it does today.
 “While this decline was expected, revenue is declining faster than anticipated with drops both at the gas pump and at DMV—Oregon’s transportation system depends on these fees to function,” said Travis Brouwer, deputy director of the Oregon Department of Transportation. “In the next several years, transportation agencies across Oregon at the city, county and state level will have fewer dollars to maintain and improve the transportation system. With inflation rising, each of those dollars will buy less. ODOT remains committed to using resources efficiently and making them go as far as possible.”
 The decline in the State Highway Fund widens the gap ODOT is expected to face between available revenues and the cost to keep service and staffing levels stable. Earlier this year, before high gas prices and reduced vehicle registrations drove down revenue, ODOT expected to face a roughly $200 million funding gap for the 2027-2029 biennium that would require eliminating more than 500 jobs across the agency. Because of the gas tax and State Highway Fund decline, that gap has widened to $240 million, which will likely require elimination of even more jobs. These reductions come at a time when the department has already cut hundreds of millions of dollars from its budget and employs fewer people than it has at any time in the last 27 years .
 In response to this declining revenue and growing budget gap, ODOT will further reduce hiring and spending while working to maintain critical services. The agency has hired workers to be prepared for winter maintenance like snowplowing but will only hire the most critical jobs going forward.
 This new decline will also result in about $40 million fewer dollars going to cities and counties through the end of the 2027-2029 budget cycle. Local governments receive nearly half of all State Highway Fund revenue and are facing their own increasing maintenance backlogs and unfunded safety solutions.
 If funding for maintaining and operating the transportation system continues to decline, travelers will experience rougher roads, more delays, more closures, and less reliable travel across the state. To learn more about transportation funding in Oregon and efforts to put state and local transportation agencies on a sustainable path, visit ODOT’s funding page .
